items.text: The mixer was running, this low hum and stuff and the vibration going through soles of his boots. Flour dust everywhere in the air, catching the fluorescent lights like snow, kind of floating around. Was 3:17 am. The sourdough loaves sat out on wooden boards, crusts still pale and soft, not baked yet. He wiped his hands on the apron, it was stiff from dried dough and sweat. Went to check the front counter lock, just a paranoid ritual but no big deal really. So there it was. The History of Salt, hardback, blue spine cracked near the hinge. It showed up every Thursday for six weeks, sitting on the glass display case next to some unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp on it and the place isn't part of the municipal library system, which is why he was confused about it. He picked it up, the cover felt cold. Opened it. Thought maybe he'd find blank pages, a bookmark or something like that. But no, it was a folded square of lined notebook paper that fell onto the counter with a soft tap. He unfolded it. Jagged handwriting, written pretty hard into the paper. It said You knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension. He just looked at it. The mixer started another cycle. He looked at his own hands, knuckles red, dusted white. He closed the book, put it back on the glass, aligned the spine with the edge properly. Turned off the overhead light above the display, left the book sitting there in shadow.

Elias had a mixer in his bakery, industrial size, and it made this really deep hum you can feel through your boots. He was checking the front door lock because he's paranoid rather than it being actually necessary, it's all flour dust in there, catching the fluorescent light, it's 3:17 am. The loaves on the wooden boards were still very pale and soft before final bake. He wiped his hands on his apron, stiff with dried dough, he's sweaty. Then he saw this book, it was the history of salt, hardback, blue spine, hinge was cracked. And it had been showing up every Thursday for 6 weeks, always on the glass display next to the unsold cinnamon rolls, no library stamp on it. It's not a branch of municipal library or anything. And he picks it up, cover is cold, he opens it. He was expecting some blank pages or a forgotten bookmark, and instead it's like a folded square of notebook paper, a slip of lined paper. He unfolds it. Handwriting is really jagged and all pressed hard into the paper, it says, you knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right, it ruins the tension. So he looks down at his own hands, which are red-knuckled and dusted with white flour, and closes it and puts it back, aligning it with the glass display case edge, puts it back on the glass. He turns off the light above it, and the book is in shadow.

The sourdough was on its second rise when I found it. Again. Its always a Thursday, always right on the flour bin, always The Count of Monte Cristo copy with the Richmond Public Library stamp on it. Don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing them. But around 3am my brain is just yeast and caffeine so who knows. Tonight though a scrap of yellow legal paper was sticking out the top like a bookmark. Wiped my hands on the apron, left a ghostly white smudge on the dark cloth. Pulled it out. "Page 142." Spiky frantic handwriting. "Please. I think they're watching the drop box now." Cold draft swept through the kitchen, smelled of wet asphalt and rain. Looked at the darkened front windows. Just my own tired reflection staring back. Didn't open the book. Instead tucked the note back between the pages. Slid the novel into a brown pastry bag. Folded the top down twice to seal.

It was on its second rise and found it again. Sourdough. It's always Thursday, always on the flour bin, always a copy of The Count of Monte Cristo with the Richmond Public Library stamp. I don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing, but honestly around 3 AM my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine anyway. Tonight though a scrap of yellow legal paper was poking out of the top like a bookmark. I wiped my hands on my apron leaving a white smudge on the dark cloth, and pulled it out. It says Page 142. Please. I think they're watching the drop box now. The writing is frantic and spiky. A cold draft went through the kitchen smelling of wet asphalt and oncoming rain. I looked to the darkened front windows but all I saw was my own tired reflection looking back. I didn't open the book. Instead I carefully tucked the note back between pages, slid the novel into a brown pastry bag, and folded the top down twice to seal it up.

2:17 every Thursday morning she found it. Library book, bakery back step. Same book always. Field Guide to North American Moths. Library sticker was pale and ghosted. Some flour got into the jacket, it was like it had been helping. So she returned it twice but the librarians just smiled too politely. Third week she just kept it next to the rye starter and said nothing to anyone.

So tonight it rained and hit the door in the alley. Ovens breathing. She was shaping croissants. Palms pushing butter into the dough. Then the latch gave that little click. Slightly guilty. So she goes looking. No one there. Book was dry as bone on the wet concrete. So she wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. Inside between the Luna Moth and Promethea was a note. Folded once. Said: your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I’m sorry about the crumbs. So she looked at the alley. Dented milk crates, steam coming up off the drains. The city felt enormous just for a second and then it didn’t. So she tore a corner off the order pad and wrote: Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. Then put the note in the book and put the book on the warm windowsill. Opened the back door.

So at 2:17 on Thursday morning, she finds the library book on the bakery back steps. Same book every time. Moths of North America, the county library sticker is faded pale on the spine, and there is some flour on the jacket like the book was helping. She took it back to the library twice. The librarians kept politely smiling. On the third week she just kept it next to the rye starter and said nothing.

Tonight rain tapping on the alley door. The ovens are breathing. She is rolling croissants, her hands pushing butter into the dough, and then the latch made its small guilty click.

No one there. Just the book lying on the wet concrete, as dry as bone. She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it up. Between the pages of Luna Moth and Promethea she finds a paper slip, folded once.

Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until first bus. Sorry about the crumbs.

She looked at the alley, dented milk crates, steam up from the drains. For a moment the city is huge and then it’s not.

She rips the corner of an order pad and writes that the cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. Then she places the note in the book, leaves it on the warm window sill, and unlocked the back door.

I found this book. Was on the steel table by the back door. Under the bench, where the bread peels hang. "A Field Guide to Coastal Birds" the title. Inside the cover there's a library stamp. Harbor St. branch. Due March. The mail slot on that door's been nailed shut, but the hatch beside it, the flour guy used, never closed right. So eleven Thursdays she has checked. Asked day staff, checked the hatch for scratches and once stayed past 4 with her coat on. Nothing. The book appeared between 2 and 4 o'clock, she was always at the ovens when it did. Back to the door. Tonight receipt from Pells grocery folded on the oystercatcher page. Ink is blotchy where someone pressed too hard. I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want. That's what the note says. Smells like salt she thought, because the pages do. She pulled the pencil out of her apron and wrote on the back of the receipt. Bring it Thursday. I'll have a roll. Tucked it in the oystercatcher and set the book on the hatch ledge. Warm roll in paper bag. Beside it.

Book came back today but nobody admitted taking it, which is how she knows it's coming through that hatch because I looked over eleven Thursdays. She asked the day staff, she checked the hatch for scratches, she once waited past 4 pm with her coat on. And it wasn't there. But the book always ended up arriving between two and four, and she was always at the ovens with her back to the door when it did.

And tonight the grocery receipt from Pell's is folded in on the oystercatchers page, the ink has gone blotchy because someone pressed too hard. And it says, I keep meaning to take this back to the library, then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. She thought it was salt. But then I can stop if you want. And she did. Pencil from her apron, she wrote, Bring it Thursday, I'll have a roll. And she put it back at the oystercatchers, put the book on the hatch ledge, and put a warm roll in a paper bag beside it.

So its 3:40, and I am in the middle of the 2nd batch of rye proofing. But the book is back again. It was sitting by the flour bin on the back door, still cold from the alley, its jacket was plastic, and its a lib book. Its been four thursdays in a row. The same book, "A Field Guide to Night Birds", from the Eastgate Branch, its three weeks overdue, and every time I take it to the drop box on my way home, but every thursday it comes back. Like the building itself borrowed it. I wiped my hands off on my apron and opened it and an index card was folded and stuck out of the page for the Barn Owl. It says "You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until 5. I walk my mothers dog, since she cant do it anymore. I keep forgetting to return it. Maybe I don't want to keep returning it. -R." I read it twice while the oven timer was counting down. Outside, the fan was humming, pushing warm air into the dark. Then I flipped the card over, and with the grease pencil I use for marking trays, i wrote "Rye's out at 4:15". Then I tore a heel off yesterdays loaf and wrapped it in wax paper, put the book on top and propped the back door open an inch.

Marisol was there 3:40 in the morning, second rye was still proofing, and it was there. The library book next to the flour bin by the back door with the plastic jacket that's all cold from the alley. On it says Eastgate Branch, due three weeks ago. Same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds. Four Thursdays now and she's carried it to the drop box every single time. But every Thursday it's back. Like the building borrowed it from her. She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. A folded index card fell out from the page about barn owls. I leave the vent fan on. It smells like bread out in the alley till about 5. Walk mother's dog because she can't anymore. Forget to return this. Maybe not wanting to. So I left the fan running. The oven timer counts down, the fan outside is humming, pushing warm air into dark. And she turned the card and with the grease pencil she uses to mark the trays she wrote on it rye's out at 4:15. And she tore a heel off yesterday's loaf and put it in wax paper, the book on top of that, propped the back door open one inch.

Thursdays the book shows up. And not on the counter, but stuck behind flour bins by the back door like whoever drops it off knows that exact spot wouldn't be in my way. The same one every time, Field Guide to North American Moths, Elmwood branch, stamp is way old, gone violet with age, due date faded. Have I ever seen anyone leave it? Nope. And I'm down in rye dough by two o'clock, and I literally wouldn't notice a marching band, that's how busy I am. First few weeks I'd put it on the shelf next to the register. It was gone by Friday mornings. Then Thursday, again. Fine. People are weird. And I'm a guy who talks to sourdough starter, so I don't have room to judge. Tonight there's a note stuck to page 114 on luna moths. They only live a week, and don't even eat. I think that's a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see bread before it's gone? No signature. Just pencil, hard pressed. I read it twice, then a third time while the ovens were ticking, and I pulled the first loaf of the night, still crackling, and I wrapped it in brown paper and put it behind the flour bins.

Thursdays the book shows up. Not on the counter though, wedged behind the flour bins by the back door. The person who leaves it must know the spots I cant trip over. Its always the same book, Field Guide to North American Moths, Elmwood Branch, due date is stamped so old the ink went purple. I have never seen anyone bring it back. I am usually in my rye dough by 2pm and honestly I would not notice a marching band. During my first few weeks I would put it on the shelf next to the cash register. By Friday morning it was gone. Thursday it showed up again. Alright. People are weird. I talk to my starter so I am not one to judge. Tonight a note on page 114, luna moths. No name, just pencil, pressed hard. I read it twice, then a third time while ovens ticked. Then I pulled my first loaf of the night, still crackling, wrapped in brown paper, and put it behind the flour bins.
